title: The services page an education product actually needs
metaTitle: Education product services page, plainly written
excerpt: Give each offer an outcome, a boundary, and a way to start a class or a trial. Write it in a teacher's or a parent's words, not as a capability grid.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops, sorting jobs the way an offer list should.

faqs.question: What does each offer on the page need?
faqs.answer: An outcome that is a scene, a boundary that says what you will not do, and a next step that starts a class or a trial. A feature such as hints or a printable belongs inside an offer. It is not an offer by itself.

faqs.question: Should schools, families, and tutors share one grid?
faqs.answer: They can share a learning moment and still need different blocks. A family decides tonight, a teacher decides before a unit, and a school decides with privacy and a calendar. One icon grid flattens those differences.

faqs.question: What should you not promise?
faqs.answer: Learning gains you have not measured, evenings you have not returned to teachers, and a faculty you do not have. Call a practice a practice and a quiz a quiz. The trial is where a false name gets caught.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
An education product services page lists the work in a teacher's or a parent's language. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to start a class or a trial.

A grid of vague capabilities does not help. "Personalized pathways, insights, engagement, community" is how a product describes itself in a pitch. It is not how a tired adult chooses a lesson.

## Offers in their words

Start from the sentences they already say. "I need a reading practice my child can do without me teaching it." "I need one activity that fits a period and shows me who is stuck." "I need a grade's worth of lessons I can assign without building them." Those sentences are your offers. Internal names such as core, plus, and enterprise can live in the billing system. They should not be the only words on the page.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a fair test. The page should help a specific person do a task, and it should be obvious who it is for. Choosing how to start a class or a trial is the task. If a stranger cannot match their sentence to a block, the page is still a capability grid.

Use the skill and the setting. Early reading at home. Fractions in class. A tutor's week. Avoid "solution," "platform," and "experience" as the noun. A lesson, a class, a practice, a school plan. Those words have edges. A buyer can reject them for a real reason, which is better than nodding at a fog.

One offer per job. Do not split "student app" and "teacher dashboard" into two products if nobody can buy the dashboard alone. Do not merge a family practice and a district contract into one card because both are "learning." The next step is different. The boundary is different. The page should admit that.

## Outcome, boundary, next step

Each block can be three short parts. Outcome: what is true after they begin. Boundary: what this offer will not do. Next step: start a class or start a trial, and what they need in hand.

Outcome is a scene, not a promise of transformation. "A parent can start a ten-minute reading practice tonight, and the child works in the product rather than in a worksheet you have to invent." That is an outcome. "Unlock every learner's potential" is a poster. Posters do not help a parent compare you with the last app they deleted.

Boundary is the trust. You do not replace their reading curriculum. You do not provide a human tutor. You do not cover every grade. You do not show a public leaderboard. You do not require a district contract for a single classroom, or you do, and you say so. Education buyers have been disappointed by implied miracles. A limit, written in the same block as the scene, is a kindness.

Next step is a concrete start. Start a trial with an email and a child's first name, if that is enough. Start a class with a class name and a rough count. Talk to a person if the offer is a school plan, and say what to bring. Do not give every block a different inspirational verb. The site should teach one action until they are inside the product.

If a block cannot fill the three parts, it is not an offer. It is a feature. Hints, progress, and a printable can sit inside the offer they belong to. A feature card with no boundary is how the grid returns.

## Schools, families, and tutors are not one grid

These buyers share a learning moment and not much else. A family is deciding tonight. A teacher is deciding before a unit, often with no procurement office. A tutor is deciding whether the tool saves prep across several students. A school is deciding with privacy, training, and a calendar. One grid that uses the same six icons for all of them will satisfy your brand board and no one else.

Write separate blocks, even if the content library is shared. The family block talks about sessions, supervision, and canceling. The teacher block talks about the period, the roster, and what the teacher still has to do. The tutor block talks about multiple learners and whether each one can move at a different point in the skill. The school block talks about what you will not customize.

Order them by the people you can serve well now. If school sales are a hope and family trials are the product, lead with families. A school block you cannot staff should say that conversations are limited, or it should wait. A page that offers a district rollout you have never done is a services page in the worst sense: a menu of work you will improvise.

Give each block a stable name you will use in the app, in email, and on the invoice. If the nav says "For teachers" and the page says "Classroom OS," pick one. Tired people will not translate you.

## One offer, written out

Here is a shape to rewrite in your own limits.

For a classroom. Outcome: you run one activity in a normal period and see which students are stuck on the same step, without building the worksheet. Boundary: one subject, the grades you list, no guarantee of test scores, no after-school tutoring by your team. Next step: start a class. Bring the grade and a rough headcount. You do not need a purchase order to see the first lesson, if that is true.

Read it to a teacher who is not your friend. If they ask "but what is it," the outcome is still a compliment. If they ask "what does it cost," point to pricing without changing the subject. If they ask for five extra subjects you do not have, the boundary is doing its job.

Do a second block for a family, with the same honesty. Outcome, the practice and the time. Boundary, you are not the parent and you are not the whole school day. Next step, start a trial. If the trial needs a card, say it here and on the pricing page. Do not let one page be kinder than the other.

Hanabi builds marketing sites and product interfaces that can carry this kind of plain offer: the page, the signup, and the first-run screen in one design. The point for you is not a particular stack. The point is that the sentence on the services page is the sentence the product can keep on the first night.

## What the page should not promise

Do not promise learning gains you have not measured, and do not borrow a number from a neighboring product. Do not promise that teachers get their evenings back. Some time may be saved. Claiming the evening is how you get a bitter review from a teacher who still had to plan. Say the smaller thing you actually remove, such as making the practice sheet.

Do not promise a pedagogy you do not have. If the product is deliberate practice, call it practice. If it is a full lesson with a teachable explanation, call it a lesson. If it is a quiz, call it a quiz. Misnaming the work is the education version of a reel with no caption. The buyer finds out in the trial, which is the most expensive place to find out.

Do not promise humans you do not have. "Our team of educators" should be true this month. If a specialist reviews content, say what they review. If the product is software with a careful editor, say that. A phantom faculty is a claim a parent may repeat to a school. You will have to live next to it.

Keep compliance language accurate and short. If you have a privacy policy, link it. Do not invent certifications. A missing badge is better than a badge you cannot explain when an administrator asks.

## Around the list, and after it

The top of the page is two sentences. Who the offers are for, and that each one ends in a class or a trial. Do not preview every block in vaguer words. Give the page a title that says what a person can start, not a pile of synonyms. [Google's notes on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) favor a descriptive title that stays specific to the page. Use that. Let the heading be human.

Under the list, say that most people need one offer, not all of them. A parent does not need the school plan. A principal does not need to start by pretending to be a single child. Routing is a service. Confusion is not thoroughness.

End by showing the learning moment once, shared, so the blocks do not feel like different companies. One frame of the practice or the lesson. Then the actions again. If you cannot show the same product behind two offers, you may have two products, and the page should not pretend otherwise.

When you want the offers checked against what the product really does, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the grid you have now, including the icons. The useful result is fewer blocks, each with a boundary you can keep.

The people behind those offers are the next page. A clear menu can still feel like nobody stands behind the lesson. [How an education product should write an about page](/blog/how-an-education-product-should-write-an-about-page) is the piece to write next. Name who makes the lessons and why a teacher or a parent should care. Skip the origin story unless it changes the decision to start.
